item.title: When Compilers Surprise You
item.description:
Every now and then a compiler will surprise me with a really smart trick. See the video that accompanies this post. ↩ Why does the compiler emit this exact sequence and not a slightly more straightforward sequence.

HN Discussion

Read Original Article

Top 3 Comments:

andrepd:

I'm actually surprised that gcc doesn't do this! If there's one thing compilers do well is pattern match on code patterns and replace with more efficient ones; just try pasting things from Hacker's Delight and watch it always canonicalise it to the equivalent, fastest machine code.

dejj:

It’s neat. I wonder if someone attempted detecting a graph coloring problem to replace it with a constant.

mgaunard:

Those are just basic and essential optimizations, nothing too surprising here.

The sum of integers is actually a question I ask developers in interviews (works well from juniors to seniors), with the extra problem of what happens if we were to use floating-point instead of integers.

item.title: The e-scooter isn't new – London was zooming around on Autopeds a century ago
item.description:
Lady Florence Norman 1916 (street background expanded) These were the Autoped, an American import that was once popular enough to regularly appear in the newspapers before vanishing seemingly without a trace. Several noted that the owners were switching to a car instead. It seems that the British weather might have killed off the Autoped.

HN Discussion

Read Original Article

Top 5 Comments:

bondarchuk:

>"(street background expanded)"

As in... expanded using generative AI? (The perspective on the lamps is really off unless they're different size lamps)

hylaride:

> The e-scooters that clutter up pavements may seem like a new thing, but a hundred years ago, there were already people zooming around London on powered scooters.

The problem is that we've given so much space to automobiles that there's no room for anything else (bikes, scooters, etc). Pedestrians have been given a sliver only because drivers need to walk between parking and their destination. This is true even in cities where the majority of people don't even drive!

jtbayly:

No way that’s a 15 inch wheel.

thenthenthen:

These are ICE and not electric.

nickdothutton:

I also like to point out that we had electric powered food delivery services in London from 1932.

item.title: AMD entered the CPU market with reverse-engineered Intel 8080 clone 50 years ago
item.description:
Agreement with IntelIn 1976, AMD was presented with another great opportunity to profit from its clone of Intel's 8080. Am9080 chips had a significantly smaller die than the Intel 8080 that they copied. Intel’s 8080 processor SKUs were never produced with clock speeds above 3.

HN Discussion

Read Original Article

Top 1 Comments:

ksec:

If Intel decide to focus on Foundry, I just wish AMD and Intel could work together and make a subset clean up of x86 ISA open source or at least available for licensing. I dont want it to end up like MIPS or POWER ISA where everything is too little too late.

item.title: New reactor produces clean energy and carbon nanotubes from natural gas
item.description:
Credit: Nature Energy (2025). Credit: Nature Energy (2025). Credit: Nature Energy (2025).

HN Discussion

Read Original Article

Top 5 Comments:

westurner:

ScholarlyArticle: "Production of hydrogen and carbon nanotubes from methane using a multi-pass floating catalyst chemical vapour deposition reactor with process gas recycling" (2025) https://www.nature.com/articles/s41560-025-01925-3

jaggs:

Oh come on. Produces 'clean energy' from natural gas? Yeah of course.

cmrdporcupine:

When carbon byproducts are produced from these kinds of reactions, are they "pure" carbon, or will there be residues from the impurities in the methane?

The reason I ask is I wonder if the carbon could be used as a soil amendment to help replenish top soils in agriculture, or as a growing medium generally. But this would only be conceivable if it's just carbon.

showmexyz:

Math seems wrong "The team found that the loop design would convert 75% of the gas entering the system into useful resources, producing carbon nanotubes and hydrogen in a 3:1 mass ratio. In other words, for every 4 kilograms of methane the system successfully converts into useful resources, it makes 3 kilograms of nanotubes and 1 kilogram of hydrogen."

PaulHoule:

A big research area, see "Turquoise Hydrogen"

https://www.aga.org/its-time-to-pay-attention-to-turquoise-h...

in contrast to "Grey Hydrogen" [1] made by steam reforming

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_reforming

The self-taught ChemE in me worries a little about any process that makes a solid product since that product could plate out inside the machine and clog it up, but maybe that's not really a problem here.

[1] "Blue" if you capture the CO2
